title: Those who disagree
tomorrow: can Sofia's dad forgive his brother before he feels like it?

cards: A family dinner, and someone says the thing you think is flat wrong. You can feel the eye-roll start before you decide to do it. So can you disagree with someone and still respect them?

The Bible doesn't pretend the first Christians agreed. In Acts, Paul and Barnabas, partners on the road, argue over whether to bring a young man named Mark. Acts calls it a sharp disagreement, and they split up.

teach.b: That's not where it ends. Years later, writing to Timothy, Paul asks for Mark by name: bring him, he's useful to me. The split didn't turn into contempt.
The disagreement was real, and so was the respect underneath it. Saint Ignatius of Loyola wrote a rule for this at the start of his Spiritual Exercises, and the Catechism repeats it.
Be readier to find a good meaning in what someone says than to condemn it. If you can't, ask them how they mean it.

teach.h: THEN ASK. THEN CORRECT WITH LOVE.
teach.b: And if they really are wrong, correct them with love. Notice the order: first the best reading, then a question, and only then the correction.

Contempt skips the first two steps and goes straight to the eye-roll. This week's people all needed that order: the enemy you pray for, the stranger you don't know yet, the poor man whose name you never asked.
Disagreeing well is one more way of looking at a person before deciding about them.

how: People who make an Ignatian retreat meet Ignatius's presupposition about reading others charitably near the start of the Spiritual Exercises, and the Catechism repeats it in its teaching on truthfulness.

o: people who leave the Church over a dispute
people you argue with and still respect
anyone whose opinions you're allowed to ignore

games.q: two weeks of people — tap the pairs.
p: lay not this sin to their charge
became a neighbor on his road
the poor man with a name

s: respecting someone means never disagreeing with them
Paul and Barnabas disagreed sharply, and Paul later asked for Mark by name.
Ignatius said to correct a wrong idea right away and firmly
first look for the good meaning, then ask how they mean it, then correct with love.
in Luke's story, the rich man knew Lazarus's name
he asks Abraham to send Lazarus.

games.q: in class, someone argues the opposite of you on something you care about. going by Ignatius's rule, what comes first?
o: correct the mistakes in their facts right away.
look for the best version of their point, then ask.
stay quiet; disagreeing out loud is disrespectful.
games.why: Ignatius's order is the good reading first, then a question, then a correction with love. silence isn't respect, and speed isn't truth.

practice: Bring to mind a view you strongly disagree with, held by someone you know. Then say out loud, in one quiet sentence, the best version of it, the way its most thoughtful believer would put it.
Notice how it feels to say it fairly, and let that sit for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: Those who disagree. People you can argue with and still respect, the way Paul came back around to Mark. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: without contempt. The best reading first, then a question, then love. Two weeks of people, done.
